paragraphs.heading: What the idea says
paragraphs.text: Mass–energy equivalence is the link between an object's mass and its energy, taken in the object's rest frame, the viewpoint in which it sits still. Einstein summed it up in the formula E = mc², where E is energy, m is mass and c is the speed of light. Mass and energy differ only by a constant multiplier and by the units used to measure them. So anything with mass carries its own built-in energy, even when it is not moving at all.

paragraphs.heading: Why a little mass goes a long way
paragraphs.text: The speed of light is a big number, and the formula squares it. That means a small amount of mass matches an enormous amount of energy. For one kilogram, mc² comes to something on the order of 10¹⁷ joules. The chemical or heat energy stored inside an ordinary resting object tends to be far smaller than that.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy goes
paragraphs.text: When a chemical or nuclear reaction loses some mass, a matching amount of energy is let out. In a nuclear reaction, the atoms that come out have less mass than the atoms that went in. The missing mass turns up as heat and light carrying the equivalent energy. To work this out, E is read as the energy released and m as the change in mass.

paragraphs.heading: Adding and removing energy
paragraphs.text: The rule also runs the other way. All the energy that travels along with an object adds to its total mass, which measures how hard the object is to speed up. Imagine an isolated box of perfect mirrors that could hold light: the photons have no mass one by one, yet together they add their energy divided by c² to the box's mass. Taking energy out removes mass by m = E/c², and putting energy into an isolated system raises its mass by the same amount.

paragraphs.heading: Rest mass and moving mass
paragraphs.text: Physicists talk about two kinds of mass. Rest mass, also called invariant mass, is the mass an object has when it is not moving relative to the observer, and it does not depend on how the observer moves. Relativistic mass does change with motion: a moving object has more of it because it has kinetic energy, the energy of motion, so different observers get different values. Since relativistic mass is really just energy under another name, physicists usually keep the word mass for rest mass.

paragraphs.heading: A whole is not its parts added up
paragraphs.text: One surprise is that masses do not simply add. The parts of a system pull on each other, which gives them potential energy, and the rest mass of the whole counts all the energy of its parts, including their motion. So in general an object's mass is not the total of its pieces' masses. The plain sum only works when the parts are at rest and neither attract nor repel each other.

paragraphs.heading: Where it came from
paragraphs.text: In the late 1800s, people explored some connection between mass and energy under the name electromagnetic mass. The French polymath Henri Poincaré described it as a paradox arising from special relativity. Einstein was the first to put it forward as a general principle that follows from the symmetries of space and time. It appeared in his paper of 21 November 1905, and today it is basic to nuclear and particle physics.
